articles.title_orig: FTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricing
articles.title_zh: FTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricing
articles.content_orig:
Regulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or service
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is demanding some of the US’s biggest airlines, ride-share companies and retailers divulge how they are using algorithms and loyalty programs to target customers and drivers with different prices and wages.
Nine companies – Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart – were named in the inquiry, which comes after investigations and lawsuits alleging consumers are charged different prices based on their buying histories and drivers paid different fares based on their personal histories.
The FTC will “scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service”, chair Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.
US family budgets already burdened by inflation are being gouged by opaque and sometimes deceptive store pricing practices, including surveillance pricing and overcharges by Dollar General and convenience stores .
The FTC is tasked with policing “unfair or deceptive acts or practices” in industries except banking and airlines, which means it can not impose any fines or regulations on the airlines named. While the Trump administration has rolled back corporate regulations, the FTC’s consumer protection division has joined with states in some instances to pursue legal action and penalties against some companies.
Companies must “turn over information that will allow the agency to assess whether the pricing for a ticket, ride share, food delivery or other product or service varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data by super-intelligence algorithms”, the FTC said.
Several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels that could be used to set different prices based on shoppers habits and online information.
The probe follows a July 2024 inquiry by the Biden administration into surveillance pricing, which demanded information from McKinsey, JPMorgan Chase and others that offered surveillance pricing products to consumer-facing companies.
“Details like a person’s precise location or browser history can be frequently used to target individual consumers with different prices for the same goods and services,” the FTC found in January of 2025.
Whether the inquiry will result in substantial changes in consumer laws or company practices is unclear.
“What we have seen so far is that they have not been using these studies that produce meaningful reports that ultimately lead to any rule-making changes,” said Rohit Chopra, a former FTC commissioner who is now head of California’s new Business and Consumer Protection Agency.

articles.title_orig: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.title_zh: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.content_orig:
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

articles.title_orig: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street bought Microsoft and sold Alphabet after the two reported quarterly earnings Wednesday night. Both rent computing power to the AI labs and own stakes in them, but this quarter Microsoft cashed in while Alphabet's bets cost it.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) stock rose about 2% after hours, while Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) fell over 9%, on track for its worst day since October 2023, after its sales came up short .
For Microsoft, the labs show up as sales. OpenAI paid it $10 billion in the quarter that ended in September, according to Microsoft's quarterly filing. That's about 11% of Microsoft's $92 billion in revenue, and more than its Xbox and Windows businesses brought in combined.
Some of that money is still owed. OpenAI's unpaid bills to Microsoft rose to about $7 billion from $6 billion three months earlier. Microsoft also owns about 24% of the ChatGPT maker, but the stake barely moved its profit this time.
The order book cooled, too. Microsoft's backlog — revenue customers have signed up for, but Microsoft hasn't yet booked — slipped to about $677 billion, and new bookings fell 12% from a year earlier. CFO Amy Hood blamed "large Azure commitments in the prior year" for the tough comparison.
Alphabet's bets on the labs worked the other way. Its stakes in other companies, including roughly 14% of Anthropic and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ), supplied about $6 of its $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter.
This time they cost it. A nearly $9 billion loss on those holdings cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the call that the loss came "primarily" from SpaceX, whose stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Alphabet is also footing the bill to build. It spent $51 billion on data centers and equipment in the quarter, more than double a year earlier, and burned about $9 billion in free cash flow — the cash left after those investments — for a second straight quarter. Microsoft generated about $19 billion and said it expects to stay positive this fiscal year.
To cover the gap, Alphabet bought back no stock, sold about $29 billion of bonds and $12 billion of new shares, and nearly tripled its long-term debt this year to about $125 billion. Meta ( META ) took a similar route with its nearly $100 billion stock sale .
The payoff is showing up in Google Cloud, where revenue doubled to about $31 billion and the backlog of signed contracts rose to $561 billion from $514 billion three months earlier. Anthropic has committed at least $115 billion to Google for computing power, according to its IPO filing, about a fifth of that backlog by Yahoo Finance calculations.
The next swing could come from Anthropic itself. Its IPO could start trading as soon as Nov. 16 , and once it does, Alphabet's stake gets valued at the market price each quarter. At the reported $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation, that could turn the drag back into a windfall by year-end.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella doesn't want to lean on the labs forever. Asked on the call where Azure's AI growth is coming from, he said he's after breadth, not "four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth."
"That's not a business as far as I'm concerned," he said.

articles.title_orig: Xbox consoles get a massive October 2026 update adding loads of new features
articles.title_zh: Xbox consoles get a massive October 2026 update adding loads of new features
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft has started rolling out the October 2026 Xbox console update, bringing 10 new features, dashboard improvements, and several bug fixes to Xbox consoles.
The update began reaching players on October 28, following testing with Xbox Insiders. Major additions include Mythic Achievements, customizable startup animations, improved game save management, and higher-quality Remote Play.
According to the official Xbox update notes , one of the biggest additions is Mythic Achievements , which reward players who unlock every original achievement in a game. DLC and post-launch achievements do not count, and players keep their Mythic status permanently once they earn it.
Microsoft has also improved the Disc-to-Digital License Portal , allowing players to manage inaccessible licenses directly on their consoles instead of opening a webpage. Players can also view, sort, and delete unused local game saves to free up storage.
Another addition lets Xbox owners choose different startup animations , including designs from the Xbox One era through the latest generation. Xbox Series X|S also gains Remote Play support for streaming up to 1440p with higher video bitrates on compatible devices.
The update improves party chat reliability and security while giving players more control over their dashboards. Users can remove games and apps from their recent activity lists or press the Right thumbstick on Home to hide dashboard elements and display their background.
Microsoft has also added search options within My games & apps, achievement lists, and player profiles. Cloud-played games now appear automatically in My games & apps, while downloads can continue during cloud streaming when network conditions allow.
Finally, Xbox profile badges now show sharper images and more details about when and how players earned them.
Beyond the new features, the October update addresses several problems affecting console performance and usability.
Microsoft has fixed an issue that caused the Home screen to refresh continuously, along with a separate problem that sometimes left consoles displaying a black screen during startup.
The update also resolves unexpected download interruptions, missing images and text for certain compilation discs, and selection focus problems in My games & apps.
Players with large game libraries should also see improved memory management, stability, and performance.
Players can check for it manually by opening Settings > System > Updates and installing any available system update.
Those who prefer automatic updates can leave their consoles configured to download and install system updates as Microsoft continues the rollout.

articles.title_orig: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
articles.title_zh: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), less than a week after Seoul proposed talks over a growing border dispute.
The missiles were launched at about 12:30pm (03:30 GMT) on Thursday from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement.
Japan’s Defence Ministry separately confirmed the launch of what it said could be a ballistic missile that fell outside the country’s Exclusive Economic Zone, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The launch comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border between the two Koreas, on September 21.
A joint South Korea-United Nations investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago,with Seoul calling for an apology.
Pyongyang rejected the finding, sending a letter to the UN Security Council (UNSC) this week accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion.
The North Korean permanent representative to the UN, Kim Song, wrote about the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.
Song told the UNSC that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, labelled South Korean demands for an apology as “despicable” while separately rejecting an offer of medical equipment from Seoul.
South Korea has proposed military talks with its neighbour in a bid to calm the situation.
Seoul said last Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.
It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.
The ratcheting tensions come as United States President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that US ally Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
Pyongyang launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim this year.

articles.title_orig: Samsung is killing another key Galaxy service
articles.title_zh: Samsung is killing another key Galaxy service
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Samsung is surprisingly streamlining its secondary service footprint, recently shuttering services like Samsung Daily Plus and overhauling backend platforms like Samsung Community . It now seems Samsung News is next on the chopping block.
Samsung has announced that it will officially discontinue Samsung News on December 21, 2026. According to an official in-app notice spotted by SamMobile , Samsung News will stop delivering content entirely on the shutdown date.
The standalone widget will no longer receive updates, and Samsung recommends that users of Galaxy phones and tablets remove it from their home screens. The leftmost swipe panel on the One UI home screen, which previously hosted Samsung News alongside Google Discover, will likely default to Google Discover exclusively.
Samsung further noted that any personal information collected through the service will be deleted upon termination, retaining only records required by applicable local regulations.
Launched in 2023, Samsung News was the tech giant’s latest attempt to build a viable rival to Google Discover and Apple News, replacing the older Samsung Free (and Samsung Daily and Bixby Home before that). Despite revamping the reading experience with curated daily briefings and partner syndication, the platform never quite managed to unseat Google Discover as the default feed for most Galaxy users.
Samsung has not announced a replacement news aggregator, signaling that the company is stepping away from standalone content curation on Galaxy devices.

articles.title_orig: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.title_zh: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
While Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is getting a pass.
Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't trading down in sympathy. And there is one simple reason why this is the case.
Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters.
Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations. Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points.
The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside. Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts.
"Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback.
Alphabet shares tanked 10% in pre-market trading after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.
"Alphabet's 3Q results reinforced concerns we had heading into the print, re: Search is decelerating and margins have peaked near-term. This could create an air pocket over the next 1-2 quarters as investors await signs for whether this is transitory or structural," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.title_orig: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.title_zh: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.title_zh: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX took its worst one-day hit last Thursday since early August, when its biggest share unlock yet freed up to 1.3 billion shares to trade. Roughly a week later, it's back at the same floor, and the rest of the space trade has left it behind.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) shares slipped again on Thursday during premarket trading, along with nearly every space stock.
$140 has been SpaceX's floor since the summer. It marked the top of the stock's August trading range before a breakout, and it sits about halfway between the August low near $108 and the $172 ceiling that capped rallies in June and October.
That makes $140 support , a price where buyers have repeatedly stepped in. They did it twice this month, and the stock is back there again.
SpaceX fell about 9% on Oct. 22 as those shares unlocked.
Since then, the smaller names have done the running. Rocket Lab ( RKLB ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ), Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ) and AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) gained roughly 8% to 14% from the Oct. 22 close through Tuesday, while SpaceX barely budged.
That bounce followed a much rougher month for the group: over the past 30 days, those four are down roughly 20% to 35%, compared with a loss of about 3% for SpaceX.
The pullback comes as investors gear up for Anthropic's IPO, the next mega-listing, with JPMorgan again set to lead retail share sales as it did for SpaceX. SpaceX sits about a third below its June record close near $212.
A sustained break below $140 would open the door to a deeper slide toward the August low near $108. To turn the chart around, bulls first need to get back above the 50-day moving average, near $150, before taking another run at $172.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) report after the bell. How much more they plan to spend building AI data centers is the number most likely to move a stock that's now mostly an AI company .

articles.title_orig: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
A drone operator with the military call sign Professor operates a Lupynis-10-TFL-1 from The Fourth Law at a test site in central Ukraine. Paula Bronstein/for NPR hide caption
KYIV, Ukraine — Like many tech entrepreneurs in Ukraine, Yaroslav Azhnyuk turned to developing drone warfare after Russia's 2022 invasion.
Drones have transformed the way wars are fought. Azhnyuk says artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable.
"When the other side has orders of magnitudes higher capabilities, it gives you an asymmetric advantage," he says. "It can make you 10,000 times more effective."
Azhnyuk runs the Ukraine-based defense firms The Fourth Law and Odd Systems. They are among the top companies producing AI-powered drones in Ukraine. Dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, called the Lupynis-10-TFL-1.
Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine. AI warfare is part of a high-tech arms race that has many worried, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.
Azhnyuk told NPR that he acknowledges the concern over destructive weapons but says it's not specific to AI.
"It has been with humanity since the invention of fire or steel," he says. "Any kind of tool can be used for good or for bad. And in the end, it's the human that decides how to use that tool."
Cameras that "fling explosives"
Azhnyuk is 37, a gregarious computer scientist who hails from a family of scholars and scientists. NPR meets him in a conference room in Kyiv; for security reasons he asked us not to reveal much else about the location.
He worked for years in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including Petcube , which makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and even entertain pets while they're alone.
"These cameras allow pet parents to watch pets when they're not at home," he says, "and fling treats to them and shine a laser toy for them. We sold a million of these devices that are quite popular in the U.S."
After Russia launched its full-scale war, Azhnyuk, by then living in Ukraine, pivoted to the defense space.
"I was like, OK, I've got to move on from Petcube and do something to protect my country," he says. "And so now we're making not cameras that fling treats but cameras that fling explosives at people who came to occupy our land."
The cameras he's talking about are part of an image recognition system incorporated into first-person-view or FPV drones.
"We are leaders in autonomous drones and thermal cameras," he says.
A Lupynis-10-TFL-1 drone is seen in the air at a test site in central Ukraine. Paula Bronstein for NPR hide caption
A drone named after a poet
The autonomous Lupynis TFL-1 drone combines a small, affordable FPV drone with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. That means the drone has an onboard computer and AI technology that takes control during the last 500 meters (or 0.3 miles) of the flight.
"But it's very different from, say, the kind of AI that sits on those data centers that power Claude," he says. "Or even the kind of AI that does self-driving for your Tesla."
Azhnyuk says this AI technology uses simple tools to recognize images and make smart software "which then allows you either to navigate autonomously without a human or to choose a target autonomously or to fly toward the target autonomously."
The Fourth Law's autonomous drone is named after the 20th century Ukrainian poet and political activist Anatoliy Lupynis, who endured decades of Soviet imprisonment and psychiatric torture. The company named all its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians in the last century.
"It is important for us to help to resurrect those people," Azhnyuk says. "Their ideas are still with us. And now they're fighting back."
"The drone is doing everything itself"
The Fourth Law teams test the Lupynis TFL-1 drones every day. We meet one team in an overgrown field outside Kyiv. They've set up a fold-out table near a copse of trees and a hornets' nest.
A slight, sandy-haired man stands up from the fold-out table and says he's the head of the test and integration team. He uses the military call sign Stab. The Fourth Law asked NPR not to reveal this location or the identities of those who work here for security reasons.
"So you see here is our camera, plus the microcomputer inside this 3-D model," Stab says. "All of the mind is here," he adds with a laugh.
The microcomputer inside the drone runs on a deep-learning neural network that uses hours of combat footage to recognize targets.
"Like vehicles, light-armored vehicles, tanks, and flying objects," he says.
The drone begins its flight guided by a pilot, who also asked us to use his call sign, Professor. He navigates the drone with a control stick. He selects a target and checks a video monitor. Then he sees a red flash.
"That means it has locked," Stab says.
The drone has locked onto its target: a dilapidated car an employee is driving along a dirt road. Professor lets go of the control stick. The drone flies itself to the car. The microcomputer inside constantly runs algorithms to keep it on course.
"See, Professor is doing nothing, and the drone is doing everything itself," Stab says.
On the battlefield, the drone would carry an explosive to hit the car. The test drone doesn't have one.
Stab says AI drones are useful because they're hard to jam. He also insists safeguards are in place so The Fourth Law drones won't go rogue. Humans select the target, he says.
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, the founder of the AI drone company The Fourth Law, previously worked in Silicon Valley and started several companies, including one that makes smartphone-powered cameras that use artificial intelligence to watch and entertain pets while they're alone. Paula Bronstein/for NPR hide caption
Survival vs. the ethics of AI
Back in the conference room, Azhnyuk says his company's AI-powered drones are not killer robots.
"They're very far from a Terminator kind of scenario, right?" he says. "These are just sort of calculators. Like they're no more likely for a Terminator uprising than a warehouse with artillery shells."
He does acknowledge, though, that AI is developing quickly. "It's not unthinkable," he says, "to imagine that some years in the future there will be drones that will be able to make their own decisions on designating targets or not."
That's the future. Right now he is focused on what Ukraine needs today.
"Our adversaries are using the very same technologies, and if they use AI for decision-making in an offensive scenario, and if we refuse to use AI in decision-making in a defensive scenario, we've lost, right?" he says. "Because their systems are capable of making decisions in microseconds, and human control takes minutes, hours and sometimes days."
If Ukraine loses, he says, "there's no way for us to argue about the ethics of AI."
The most important thing, he says, is don't die.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this story from Kyiv.

articles.title_orig: Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers
articles.title_zh: Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers
articles.content_orig:
COLMA, CALIFORNIA - JANUARY 06:  Ford pickup trucks are displayed on the sales lot at Serramonte Ford on January 06, 2026 in Colma, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.
American automakers are reporting their third quarter earnings, and they're saying revenues are up, but they're also facing some serious headwinds.
Or as Mike Wall, an analyst at the automotive data company Mobility Global, put it: If this year was a book about the auto industry, "It would be a mix of suspense and thrills and maybe a little bit of comedy and a little bit of horror."
For the thrills: Auto companies are doing well when it comes to selling big cars and light-duty trucks. General Motors reported its sales of light-duty trucks rose 9% in the past year . Ford's F-Series trucks continue to be a company bestseller . Stellantis' pickup sales in the U.S. rose 34% .
And revenues overall are up: General Motors reported its revenue was up 2.9% in the past year; for Ford it was a 2% rise and Stellantis was up 1% .
To analysts, all of this signals that consumers are still buying vehicles — despite concerns about affordability. The average new vehicle transaction price was just over $50,000 in September, close to a record high, according to the Kelley Blue Book . Broadly speaking, customers are paying more for high-end trims and for bigger vehicles, which tend to be more profitable for the auto companies.
"Customers have been resilient amid higher fuel prices, interest rates and inflation," said Sherry Ann House, Ford's chief financial officer, on a call with investors.
But now for the suspense: The Detroit Three automakers are also cautioning investors that it's getting more expensive to make cars. Key materials like steel, copper and computer chips have all gotten pricier.
"Should we see prices at this level, it makes that more challenging heading into next year," Paul Jacobson, the chief financial officer of General Motors, said on the company's earnings call.
On the call for Stellantis, which owns Chrysler and Jeep, CEO Antonio Filosa noted that higher prices for memory chips and other raw materials "will be an industry-wide phenomenon to work with."
Since 2025, the Trump administration has put additional tariffs on imported materials like steel, aluminum and copper. Much of a car's frame — and weight — is steel. So are nuts and bolts.
Copper , critical for a car's wiring and for electric vehicle batteries, has also grown more expensive — both because of tariffs and because there's more global demand for it, especially as the need for EV batteries grows. Plus, copper wire is also in high demand for data centers.
Then there are the costs of computer memory chips , which are used in a car's electronics, and are more expensive due to a tight supply chain and demand from many industries, including from AI.
Plus, there are other logistics costs. To bring vehicles from factory floors to dealerships, they get shipped on trucks, many of which run on diesel. The average price for a gallon has been hovering around $6.35, just short of its September all-time high, according to AAA.
High diesel prices play out in other ways too. The U.S. and Canada have closely intertwined auto supply chains and parts often cross the border several times as they get shaped into a car. That movement becomes more expensive when fuel is pricier — and when the U.S. tariffs Canadian goods .
"Higher fuel prices are impacting our freight and energy costs. But notably, we are not seeing it impact customer demand for trucks and fleet vehicles at this point," said House, the CFO of Ford.
In a report to investors , General Motors forecast that the cost of materials including computer chips and diesel would run the company as much as $2 billion this year. GM is also still paying about $2.5 billion in tariff costs, Jacobson said — which was lower than the company's earlier forecasts, partially offset thanks to tariff refunds.
In Ford's earnings call, CEO Jim Farley noted a similar figure: "We currently expect commodities, memory and logistics costs to represent a year-over-year headwind of about $2 billion at Ford."
Farley and House both said growth in other parts of Ford's business, as well as software services and parts, are helping offset these costs.
On their call, Stellantis executives said they would provide more information about these costs in the fourth quarter.
All of this is disruptive for an industry that is not built for high-speed changes. It takes time and money for carmakers to plan which vehicles to build, how many, and to line up supply chains.
" This is an industry that moves at a glacial pace between generations, between vehicles, between plants," said  Sam Fiorani, a vice president for Auto Forecast Solutions. "And so when you throw in tariffs and you throw in all kinds of disruptions between countries, it throws off the supply chain and the calculation for profit and loss."
This quarter marked a full year since the demise of the $7,500 federal tax credit , which incentivized car buyers to purchase electric vehicles. Congress nixed it as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the credit ended on Sept. 30, 2025.
Data from the car analytics platforms Edmunds and Cox Automotive shows that after the credit went away, EV sales dropped nationally.
Tesla, which only makes EVs, reported that their global sales fell during the quarter, compared with the same period last year.
General Motors reported that its third quarter sales were down 6% overall compared to the previous year, partly because of the "smaller EV market."
On GM's call, Jacobson singled out the end of the tax credit as a reason for lower EV sales. He said the company plans to keep making electric vehicles, and that it's "right-sizing" its capacity and aligning its production with demand. "We think with these oil prices and these fuel prices that EV penetration may continue to go up, and we want to make sure we're ready for that," he said.
On Ford's call, executives didn't address EV sales, but they were enthusiastic about the Fathom , an electric truck the company plans to make available as a pre-order in early 2027, priced under $30,000.
But there are two bright spots for automakers when it comes to EVs. First, after last autumn's drop, EV sales have leveled out. As of September, they now make up about 6% of new car sales in the U.S., according to Edmunds.
American shoppers have also taken a greater interest in hybrids, especially given high fuel prices. Sales of hybrids are up 27% in the past year, according to Edmunds.
American automakers have noticed this trend, said Wall. "We have seen more inclination and more movement towards hybrids, and some automakers are adjusting their product plans accordingly," he said. But he added, gas-powered cars are still driving the profits of the big companies.
When it comes to electric vehicles, the companies are stuck in a kind of Catch-22. On the one hand, they're international companies — and EV demand is growing globally. Over 30 percent of new cars sold in Europe last year were electric. In China, more than half were, according to the International Energy Agency .
But EV demand in the U.S. just isn't the same. American drivers have long expressed concerns about limited range , charging infrastructure, or the cost of replacing an enormous lithium-ion battery .
"The thinking 10 years ago was we're going to skip hybrids and go right to electric vehicles. So we saw a lot of investment in factories, in battery plants, in new platforms to build fully electric vehicles," Fiorani said. But "when that volume didn't show up, they had to backtrack and develop new internal combustion vehicles going forward."
Fiorani expects to see the Detroit Three automakers offer more hybrid vehicles in the coming years, he said, "because this transition towards fully electric vehicles is going to take a lot longer than

articles.title_orig: An 8-year-old girl was attacked by a wolf in a German zoo
articles.title_zh: An 8-year-old girl was attacked by a wolf in a German zoo
articles.content_orig:
An 8-year-old girl was attacked by at least one wolf inside a German zoo’s enclosure and suffered serious injuries
BERLIN -- An 8-year-old girl was attacked by at least one wolf inside a German zoo's enclosure and suffered serious injuries, officials said.
The attack occurred Wednesday during a special event for children at the Johannismühle Wildlife Park south of Berlin, Teltow-Fläming district officials said in a news release.
The girl was flown to the hospital, the news release said. A zookeeper intervened before two other girls also in the Arctic wolf enclosure were attacked. The wolves had been given water at the time.
The zoo is closed until further notice as an investigation takes place.
A wolf bit a woman in a shopping area in Hamburg earlier this year, authorities said, in what is believed to be the first such attack since wolves returned to the country in 1998.

articles.title_orig: North Korea fires missiles as row over landmine blast intensifies
articles.title_zh: North Korea fires missiles as row over landmine blast intensifies
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), less than a week after Seoul proposed talks over a growing border dispute.
The missiles were launched at about 12:30pm (03:30 GMT) on Thursday from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement.
Japan’s Defence Ministry separately confirmed the launch of what it said could be a ballistic missile that fell outside the country’s Exclusive Economic Zone, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The launch comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border between the two Koreas, on September 21.
A joint South Korea-United Nations investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago,with Seoul calling for an apology.
Pyongyang rejected the finding, sending a letter to the UN Security Council (UNSC) this week accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion.
The North Korean permanent representative to the UN, Kim Song, wrote about the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.
Song told the UNSC that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, labelled South Korean demands for an apology as “despicable” while separately rejecting an offer of medical equipment from Seoul.
South Korea has proposed military talks with its neighbour in a bid to calm the situation.
Seoul said last Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.
It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.
The ratcheting tensions come as United States President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that US ally Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
Pyongyang launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim this year.

articles.title_orig: A U.S. cruise ship suspends a global voyage due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.title_zh: A U.S. cruise ship suspends a global voyage due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
articles.title_zh: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
articles.content_orig:
A first-time mum was denied hospital meals while her baby was "fighting for her life" because she was not breastfeeding.
Sophie Price, 22, was "shocked" when staff refused to give her a meal while her daughter Florence was being treated on a paediatric ward at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen.
Despite giving birth in the hospital five days earlier, she was told she was no longer classed as a patient as she was not breastfeeding, so she would not be provided with meals.
Aneurin Bevan health board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and was "committed to supporting families throughout their child's stay".
"It was just an awful experience. I just needed a hot meal to keep going for my daughter," said Sophie, from Newport.
Her family said they spent more than £1,000 on food from the canteen and takeaway meals during their three-week stay at the hospital while Florence was treated.
The health board said mothers are provided with meals while under the care of hospital maternity services as both them and their baby are classed as patients, whether they are breastfeeding or not.
But on paediatric wards, only the child is classed as the patient, however the hospital's policy is to provide breastfeeding mums with meals as this directly supports the baby's feeding and nutrition.
For babies who are formula-fed, the health board said formula was "provided as needed" by the hospital, but Sophie said she was told she would need to bring it in herself.
Sophie had only left the hospital - which earlier this week denied online claims it was "dangerous" and "dreadful" - for 24 hours before she and her husband Ryli Price had to return when they realised Florence was not able to breathe and the "colour started to drain from her".
"Florence started to make some really harsh grunting sounds, it sounded like a death rattle coming from her chest up into her mouth," she said.
Sophie ran into the A&E department screaming "she's not breathing" and credited the quick response of medical staff who helped save her daughter's life.
Florence was diagnosed with bronchiolitis , rhinoviruses - which causes the common cold - and a blood infection, which meant her lungs could not operate on their own.
She was placed on a machine that pumped air into her lungs via a mask.
Sophie said despite being "hungry and exhausted" she was denied a meal while her daughter was "in intensive care fighting for her life".
"Imagine being in a hospital with your seriously ill baby on breathing support monitors, overwhelmed with worry, anxiety and stress, only to be told you aren't entitled to a meal because you're formula feeding instead of breastfeeding," she said.
Sophie said she was bleeding through her clothes and "in a lot of pain" as her hips had to be put back in place after being dislocated during childbirth.
She also had a build-up of fluid in her feet called oedema , adding: "My feet, they were the size of elephant trunks to the point where I couldn't even walk from the one corridor to the next."
Sophie said she and Ryli were told Florence may need to be induced into a coma at any point and it was "so touch-and-go the whole time".
At one point, Sophie said she realised she had not eaten for about 28 hours and remembered seeing a food trolley being brought round to mums on the ward.
She said: "I remember them saying to me 'oh hi mum, hope you're OK, are you hungry?' And me saying 'oh yeah, I'm absolutely starving, I haven't eaten in ages. What have you got'?'"
Sophie was asked if she was breastfeeding, which she had not been able to do after the first 24 hours of Florence's life as she was no longer taking to her breast milk.
She explained this to staff and said Florence was being given formula, only to be told she was not able to have any food,
"I remember just being so shocked. It was so horrific," Sophie said, adding she already felt "disappointed" at being unable to breastfeed.
Due to her husband's paternity leave coming to an end, Sophie said she had "never been in such a vulnerable situation" and relied on family members to finish work and bring her food while she stayed at Florence's bedside.
Sophie's mother contacted the hospital about the issue, so it continued providing formula for Florence.
Sophie called the policy "outdated" and said it discriminated against formula-feeding mothers "who are doing their very best in difficult circumstances".
She thinks all hospitals should provide meals for mothers, regardless of how they are feeding their babies.
The health board thanked Sophie for her feedback and said it understood "how difficult and stressful it can be for parents when their child is in hospital".
It added: "Where parents are unable to access the hospital canteen, have limited support, or are unable to leave their child's bedside, ward teams can provide a selection of basic food items and refreshments to help meet immediate needs.
"Parents can also access a discounted hospital meal through a ward voucher scheme and where a family is experiencing financial hardship, support can be discussed with the ward team.
"Requests are considered on a case-by-case basis to ensure help is provided fairly and appropriately, taking account of the family's circumstances and the needs of the child."

articles.title_orig: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
articles.title_zh: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
articles.content_orig:
Parents and teenagers across Northern Ireland could face significant changes to how they access social media next year, with photo identification, banking information and facial scans among the methods identified to enforce the UK Government’s planned ban for under-16s.
Communications regulator Ofcom has identified four methods capable of providing highly effective age checks, as ministers prepare to publish detailed rules before the end of 2026.
The restrictions are expected to come into force in 2027, although the Government has yet to finalise precisely how the ban will operate, which services it will cover and how users will be required to prove their age.
The proposals could affect families throughout the UK, including Ballymena and the wider Mid and East Antrim area, with many adults also potentially facing additional checks before accessing social media platforms.
Ofcom's assessment identifies four approaches currently capable of reliably establishing whether someone is aged 16 or over.
• Photo ID matching – users provide a passport, driving licence or other accepted photo identification, which is checked against a live image of their face.
• Banking-based checks – with the user's consent, platforms access age information already held by a bank or financial institution.
• Digital ID services – users verify their identity through a digital service, potentially allowing them to confirm their age repeatedly without presenting identification each time.
• Facial age estimation – technology analyses facial features to estimate a person's age, with additional verification where the result is uncertain.
These are methods identified by the regulator, rather than a final list of checks that every platform will be required to offer.
Ofcom says facial age estimation technology can be inaccurate by several years around the age of 16. It therefore recommends a system similar to the Challenge 25 approach used by retailers selling alcohol.
Under this approach, platforms would set a higher age threshold for facial estimation and require further verification where a user appears close to the minimum permitted age.
One of the challenges identified by Ofcom is that some 16- and 17-year-olds do not currently hold the identification they may need to prove they are old enough to access restricted services.
The regulator estimates that approximately 94% of people aged 16 and over in the UK hold either a passport or driving licence. However, evidence suggests around 150,000 teenagers aged 16 and 17 have neither document.
Around 90% of UK teenagers in that age group are estimated to have a bank account, potentially providing another route to age verification.
Ofcom acknowledges that some young people may need to obtain identification to access social media once the restrictions are introduced.
Options include applying for a passport, provisional driving licence or a photo identification card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme (PASS). Some PASS cards are available free to 16- and 17-year-olds, including options that do not require existing photo identification.
Although the proposed ban is aimed at children under 16, its introduction could affect adult social media users.
Ofcom says platforms may not need to carry out fresh checks where they already hold accurate and reliable information establishing that an existing account holder is above the required age.
However, many adults are still likely to be asked to verify their age, using methods available under the regulator's existing guidance for age assurance at 18.
The assessment also raises questions about privacy, particularly where checks involve facial images, identity documents or financial information.
Ofcom says the available methods can be implemented in ways that protect personal information and comply with data protection legislation. It will continue working with the Information Commissioner's Office on these issues.
The regulator acknowledges that even highly effective age verification cannot prevent every underage user from accessing restricted platforms.
It says social media companies will need to take additional measures to identify and prevent attempts to circumvent the restrictions.
These could include making it easier for users to report suspected underage accounts and using technology to identify accounts that may belong to children who have bypassed the initial checks.
Ofcom says analysing users' online behaviour cannot replace an age check at registration because it requires someone to have already accessed the platform. However, such technology could help identify underage users afterwards.
Dame Melanie Dawes, Ofcom's Chief Executive , said:
“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right. It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply.
“We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play.”
Ofcom intends to publish research examining how children circumvent the restrictions within 12 months of the ban coming into effect.
A separate Ofcom report has also raised concerns about how app stores establish children's ages.
The regulator found that three-quarters of children who use the internet reported that apps downloaded from an app store were their primary means of going online.
However, all the app stores examined currently rely on children declaring their own age, with only limited additional verification in some circumstances.
Ofcom believes app stores could contribute to stronger online protections by introducing more reliable age checks, alongside better information about the risks individual apps pose to children.
App stores are not currently regulated under the Online Safety Act, and any decision to bring them within a future regulatory framework would be a matter for Government.
The regulator also suggests that protections operating across apps, devices and operating systems could be more effective than relying on individual social media platforms alone.
The Government announced its intention to introduce a ban for under-16s in June, drawing on Australia's approach while proposing stronger requirements for age verification.
Ministers intend to publish the first regulations before the end of this year, after which Ofcom will consult on detailed guidance for social media companies.
The regulator says it will be ready to take enforcement action against companies that fail to comply when the restrictions take effect in 2027.
For parents and young people in Northern Ireland, the key outstanding questions are which platforms will be covered, how existing accounts will be handled and what identification users will actually need. Those answers will depend on the final regulations, which have yet to be published.

articles.title_orig: China-Japan flights lose nearly 700,000 seats amid political spat
articles.title_zh: China-Japan flights lose nearly 700,000 seats amid political spat
articles.content_orig:
Chinese airlines cut back the most as tensions that began almost a year ago continue to depress tourism
Airlines will cut nearly 700,000 seats from their China-Japan flights and axe more than 5,000 flights for the coming winter travel season as a nearly year-old political squabble continues to depress tourism, according to aviation data provider OAG.
During the commercial aviation industry’s winter season, October 25 through March 27, carriers allocated a combined 2,871,270 seats, compared with 3,554,167 in the same season last year, OAG data showed.
The same airlines allocated 3,889,781 seats in the six months just ended, representing a cut of more than 1 million compared with the coming winter. Summer is traditionally a busier time of year for airlines.

articles.title_orig: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
articles.title_zh: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Hundreds of World War I -era bombs, grenades and artillery shells have been uncovered by the melting of ice in Italy’s Dolomite mountains, the Italian army reports.
Weapons used by the Italian and Austrian armies during the bitterly fought White War in the region, were found in September after a period of sustained glacial ice melt.
The latest finds follow an even bigger tranche of ordnance discovered during the melting over the summer.
In a statement, Italian Army officials said: "As the ice retreats, history resurfaces - and with it, dangers from the past. More than a century later, the mountains continue to yield unexploded ordnance from the Great War."
It's expected that as climate change further melts the Dolomites glaciers , more of the White War's dangerous legacy will emerge.
The officials added: "These complex operations-carried out amidst melting glaciers, steep slopes, and high-altitude terrain-demand a high level of technical expertise and experience.
"Clearing these areas means eliminating hidden dangers and making the trails-frequented every year by mountaineers, hikers, and tourists-safer."
The "White War" was fought between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces in the freezing, rugged mountain terrain between 1915 and 1918. It included some of the most horrific conditions of the First World War, as troops dug into defensive positions and endured extreme cold amid snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
Hikers reported several sightings of unexploded bombs during the summer, mainly around Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley, in the eastern Trentino region.
The Italian army subsequently carried out searches across several high-altitude areas of Trentino-Alto Adige, where retreating glaciers and melting snow have exposed wartime explosives.
Recent operations have focused on the Care Alto and Vedretta di Lares areas of the Adamello-Brenta region in Trento, as well as Val Martello and the Stelvio area in Bolzano.
The army said munitions had also been found at Cima Tre Cannoni and along the edges of the Livrio glacier.
The army said the work aimed to make mountain environments safer for mountaineers, hikers and tourists.
The White War was fought at high altitude, where troops endured extreme cold and faced the challenges of snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
More than a century later, the retreat of glaciers is exposing remnants of the conflict, including unexploded ordnance that can pose a danger to people exploring the mountains.
The army said the risks were not always immediately visible and tended to increase with altitude.
Its campaign to locate and neutralise unexploded munitions in the region is continuing as melting ice reveals further wartime remains.

articles.title_orig: Walmart Cancels Zelda Switch 2 Pre-Orders A Day Before Release
articles.title_zh: Walmart Cancels Zelda Switch 2 Pre-Orders A Day Before Release
articles.content_orig:
The Zelda -themed Switch 2 is out this week, and Walmart has reportedly cancelled some pre-orders at the last minute.
As highlighted by Kotaku , some buyers have apparently received a message from Walmart notifying them that their pre-order has been cancelled as the item is now out of stock. They won't be charged, but this information was only shared a day before the expected arrival, so they're no longer getting a system.
Unfortunately, there are similar stories in the past about preorders being cancelled like this. Some individuals have reached out to customer service reps , with Walmart supposedly confirming it "oversold" pre-orders.
Here's one of the many customer responses to Walmart's cancellation of pre-orders:
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 854k
"This is unethical sales practice. They shouldn't allow pre-orders beyond what they can stock. This denied their competitors a sale and denied an excited customer a chance at limited edition merch. I'll try again elsewhere but think consumers should be aware."
Although the system is still "out of stock", new listings on Walmart are now showing up for higher prices on its website. As Kotaku notes, the prices attached to these listings may be "set by a third-party seller using Walmart".
While this update from Walmart is no doubt frustrating for customers who pre-ordered from this retailer, Nintendo has reiterated on a few occasions now how restocks for the Zelda-themed Switch 2 are on the way. So there might still be other ways of securing this limited edition unit.
Website Vooks.net also reports the official Nintendo Store in Australia has received additional Zelda Switch 2 stock this week.

articles.title_orig: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.title_zh: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.content_orig:
Feeling that his first contribution was far too small for such a massive undertaking, Wang quietly made a second US$1.5 donation shortly after
A boy in central China who donated 10 yuan (US$1.5) to the Three Gorges Dam project in the 1990s now works for the power grid, helping transmit the electricity it generates across the country.
Wang Yu, 47, works for the State Grid Corporation of China in his hometown of Zigui county, Hubei province, according to Hubei Daily.
In 1991, 12-year-old Wang received a daily allowance of just one yuan – barely enough to buy breakfast – at a time when his parents earned a combined monthly salary of less than 100 yuan (US$15).

Former CIA deputy director’s call to repeal Obama-era ban on economic espionage comes as Beijing rushes to protect trade secrets
A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China.
“The US lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China,” wrote David Cohen, who served as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in an article published by Foreign Affairs earlier this month.
“By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.”

articles.title_zh: Inside India newsletter: New Delhi approves $22 billion in military spending amid China border tensions
articles.content_orig:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
India, the world's fifth-largest military spender, shares a contentious relationship with two of its nuclear-armed neighbors — China and Pakistan. Last year, New Delhi carried out military strikes against alleged terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, and last week an Indian official confirmed some border clashes with China.
As tensions at its borders simmer, India this week announced plans to spend billions of dollars on procuring modern warfare equipment. From whom will it get the goods?
Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.
The world's second-largest arms importer, India, is pouring billions of dollars into modernizing its military as it seeks to counter the technological advancements of neighboring China, with whom it shares an uneasy peace.
Last week, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's north-eastern border.
Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, the director general of a division of India's central armed forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, also called China the "biggest adversary" and urged for modernization of defense equipment. "It will be difficult to compete with China using traditional methods," Kapoor said.
Following Kapoor's comments, India approved spending 2.12 trillion rupees ($22 billion) to modernize its defense equipment on Monday. The country plans to spend on long-range kamikaze drones, surveillance and strike systems, counter-drone technologies, short-range air defense, artillery, helicopters and naval platforms.
Experts told CNBC that New Delhi increasingly views Beijing as a threat, especially given the Sino-Pakistan military ties, and the latest purchases were aimed at bridging the technological gap with China.
A spokesperson for India's foreign ministry said on Friday that "the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns." Beijing responded, saying it "strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries."
India's military policies are largely driven by its long-standing conflict with Pakistan, and an "increasing perception of China as a threat," Pieter Wezeman, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told CNBC.
According to a SIPRI report earlier this year, 61% of Chinese arms exports were supplied to Pakistan between 2021 and 2025.
India's latest weapons purchases will involve importing components and technology from South Korea for the artillery, engines and avionics from France for the helicopters, and drones from the U.S. and Israel, Wezeman said.
Collaboration with Russia and Japan could also be on the cards, given India's need for a technological upgrade.
Since April, India has greenlighted military spending totaling 3.7 trillion rupees, which is more than 50% of the 6.73 trillion rupee worth of approvals — a 10-year high — in the financial year ended March 2026, Citi said in a report on Tuesday.
While New Delhi has said it plans to procure 82% of the defense equipment from local industries, foreign companies are likely to play a key role in providing technology crucial for military modernization.
Foreign partnerships remain important for technologies that India does not yet produce independently, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo, told CNBC. India relies on imported technologies for specialized components such as aircraft engines, propulsion systems, sensors and electronic subsystems, he explained.
"American, Israeli, and Russian defense manufacturers are likely to find substantial opportunities in India's expanding defense market," through joint ventures, co-production and technology partnerships with Indian companies, Chaturvedi said.
India was the world's second-largest importer of major arms in 2021–25 with an 8.2% share of total global imports, even as its reliance on overseas suppliers dropped by 4% during the same time due to growing local design and production abilities, according to SIPRI.
New Delhi is also the world's fifth-largest military spender, with $92 billion, but this is less than 30% of Chinese military expenditure and around a 10th of America's, Wezeman of SIPRI pointed out.
India faces some practical challenges in matching China's scale of military modernization, but the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have shown that mass-produced systems like drones can address asymmetry, Collin Koh Swee Lean, a senior fellow at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, said.
